title: Rorty
keyWorks: Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979)
summary: Richard Rorty was an American philosopher who carried on the pragmatist tradition of James and Dewey. He held that language is not a mirror of reality but a set of tools, and that we have no final, eternal answers. Instead he proposed living with "irony" towards our own convictions, creating ourselves through new descriptions, and building solidarity by trying to reduce cruelty and humiliation.
onEmotions: Rorty didn't develop a separate theory of emotions, but his ideas change a lot about how we can look at feelings. He believed we describe ourselves with a "final vocabulary" — words like "good", "real", "loser", beyond which our explanations usually don't go. The "ironist" understands that her vocabulary is only one of many and that one can "redescribe" oneself. So no painful description of yourself is the final truth. At the same time, Rorty stressed that pain and humiliation are what all human beings share, and that solidarity is born of attention to the particular details of other people's suffering.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is understandable: the future is unclear, and you want a firm guarantee that everything will be all right. Rorty, an heir to the American pragmatism of James and Dewey, believed precisely that the world issues no such guarantee. There is no "view from nowhere" from which one could check once and for all what will happen. The pragmatists proposed looking at beliefs differently: not as mirror copies of reality but as tools for action. Seen this way, one could say that anxiety often demands the impossible — final certainty before a step is taken. Rorty suggested changing the question: not "is it true that everything will end badly?" but "which description of the situation will help me take the next step?" The anxiety doesn't vanish, but it stops being a verdict and becomes one of the voices in a conversation.
anxiety.practice: Write down the anxious thought. Then, next to it, two other descriptions of the same situation. Mark which of the three helps you most to take one small step.

fear.text: Fear is the natural reaction of a creature that can be hurt. For Rorty, it is not a shameful weakness but perhaps the most common thing that people share. He believed we have no common "human essence" to lean on, but we do share vulnerability: all of us can suffer pain and humiliation. It is on this, for Rorty, that solidarity is built — on the ability to see others as "fellow sufferers". From this point of view, your fear doesn't separate you from people; on the contrary, it connects you with them: many others are afraid of something similar right now. Fear shows what is vulnerable and precious to you. You don't have to hide it; you can acknowledge it — and let it remind you that you are not the only one who gets scared.
fear.practice: Think of one person who is probably afraid of something similar. What would you want to say to them? Perhaps it's worth saying to yourself as well.

sadness.text: Sadness needs no justification. Reading Freud, Rorty stressed that every human life is idiosyncratic — made of its own connections, memories and words, unlike any other. Freud, as Rorty saw it, let us see any life as a kind of poem rather than as a particular case of a general formula. So sadness doesn't have to be filed under a general label like "something is wrong with me". You can look at it in detail: what exactly is it about, what images and places are tied to it? Rorty generally trusted the particular more than the general — the novel more than the treatise. When sadness gets its own precise words, it becomes part of your story rather than an impersonal verdict. You can live it as a chapter that has its own meaning, even if that meaning isn't clear yet.
sadness.practice: Describe your sadness not in general words but with three concrete details: an image, a place, a sound or smell connected with it.

grief.text: Grief is one of the hardest things a person goes through, and no philosophy should hurry it. Rorty offered no metaphysical consolations: he didn't promise a reunion in another world or say that loss "has a higher meaning". But there is something important in his view of the human being. Rorty described the self as a web of beliefs, desires and words that we weave together with other people. Seen this way, one could say that the person you have lost remains woven into this web: in your words, jokes, habits, in the way you look at the world. This doesn't cancel the pain of their absence. But it means that loss doesn't erase what was between you: it goes on speaking through you.
grief.practice: Write down one word, phrase or habit you received from this person. Simply note that it is with you.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and in it it's easy to believe that you are cut off from others by your very nature. Rorty offered a different view of the bond between people. He believed that solidarity — the feeling of "we" — is not hidden in some common human essence waiting to be found. It is created: through imagination, through interest in the particular details of other people's lives, their pain and their joy. That is why Rorty valued novels and reportage so highly: they widen the circle of those we consider "one of us". Seen this way, loneliness is not a verdict on you but a state in which the bridges haven't been built yet. They are built gradually, in small steps of attention — towards others and from others. And what you are feeling now is familiar to a great many people: that is already the beginning of a "we".
loneliness.practice: Recall a book, film or story in which you recognised yourself in someone quite unlike you. What exactly brought you close?

quote.text: Solidarity is not discovered by reflection but created. It is created by increasing our sensitivity to the particular details of the pain and humiliation of other, unfamiliar sorts of people.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

anger.text: Anger is often a legitimate reaction to injustice or cruelty. Rorty himself was a politically engaged person and didn't consider indignation unworthy. Following Judith Shklar, he defined a "liberal" as someone who thinks cruelty is the worst thing we do. From this point of view, it helps to ask your anger: what particular cruelty or humiliation is it pointing to? Rorty distrusted big abstract theories and preferred gradual, concrete improvements. Anger can become the fuel for such a step. But Rorty also saw the other side: in anger it's easy to start "redescribing" the other person in humiliating terms — that is, to become a source of cruelty yourself. You can acknowledge your anger fully — and choose to let it serve the reduction of pain rather than its multiplication.
anger.practice: Put into one sentence what exactly caused the pain — without labels for the other person. What would be one small step towards putting it right?

quote.text: Liberals are the people who think that cruelty is the worst thing we do.
quote.author: Richard Rorty (following Judith Shklar)

shame.text: Shame is a very painful feeling, and it deserves gentleness. Rorty wrote a great deal about humiliation. He noticed that people can be deeply wounded by being "redescribed": by having what mattered to them made to look ridiculous or worthless. Shame is often the moment when other people's words about us become our inner verdict. But Rorty also has an answer. He believed that no language of description — neither ours nor anyone else's — is the final truth about a person. Any description can be revised. This doesn't mean nothing matters; it means that the voice shaming you is one description, not the last word. You can ask: whose language is my shame speaking? And try to talk about yourself in your own words.
shame.practice: Write down the words your shame speaks in. Think about where this language comes from. Then describe the same situation the way you would describe it for a close friend.

quote.text: The best way to cause people long-lasting pain is to humiliate them by making the things that seemed most important to them look futile, obsolete, and powerless.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that you care, and that in itself matters. Rorty didn't believe that morality descends from an eternal law or a cosmic judge. For him, obligations arise from belonging to particular "we"s — family, friends, communities — and from loyalty to them. He even described justice as "enlarged loyalty", that is, loyalty extended to an ever wider circle of people. Seen this way, one could say that guilt is not a verdict on your essence but a signal of a broken bond with particular people. And a bond, unlike a verdict, can be restored: with a word, an action, attention. Rorty was a pragmatist: he was interested not in "how bad am I" but in "what can be done next".
guilt.practice: Answer for yourself: whom, specifically, does your guilt concern? What one small step towards this person (or towards yourself) is possible now?

envy.text: Everyone knows envy, and it doesn't make you a bad person. Rorty believed there is no single scale on which human lives could be measured and compared: no "final" vocabulary that decides whose life is more right. Following the critic Harold Bloom, he wrote about the "strong poet" — someone who is frightened by the thought of being merely a copy of someone else's life and who strives to describe themselves in their own way. Seen this way, one could say that envy often measures us by someone else's yardstick. But it can also hint at something valuable: what word, what possibility you would like to see in your own story. Then it can be turned from a comparison into a question about your own language and your own life.
envy.practice: What word would you like to be able to describe your life with? Consider: is it your word, or one borrowed from the person you envy?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are heavy states; in them it's hard even to want. Rorty believed that beneath our beliefs and desires there is no hidden "true self" waiting to be found. This may sound unsettling, but it has a gentle side too: emptiness, then, is not a verdict on your essence. Rorty described language as a living process: new metaphors are born, then become familiar, "die" and turn into ordinary words. One could say that emptiness is sometimes a time when the old language you used to describe your life has worn out, and a new one hasn't appeared yet. Such transitions can be slow. They don't need to be rushed by a search for "the ultimate meaning"; it's enough to notice small glimmers of interest, from which new words grow in time.
emptiness.practice: Notice one thing today that caught your attention even a little — however small. Just write it down.

confusion.text: Confusion is unpleasant, but for Rorty it is almost the normal state of a thinking person. He introduced the notion of a "final vocabulary" — the set of words we use to justify our actions and our lives: "kind", "genuine", "right", "success". It is final because our explanations usually go no further than these words. Rorty called an "ironist" someone who understands that her vocabulary is one of many and therefore doubts it. Confusion may mean that you find yourself between vocabularies: the old words no longer hold, and new ones haven't taken shape yet. This isn't a failure but a moment of growth. Rorty didn't demand that we find a final answer; he proposed continuing the conversation and trying new descriptions until one of them starts helping you live.
confusion.practice: Write down three to five words that used to explain to you how to live and now seem to have been shaken. Don't decide anything — just look at them.

quote.text: She has radical and continuing doubts about the final vocabulary she currently uses, because she has been impressed by other vocabularies.
quote.author: Richard Rorty (on the "ironist")

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are real, and they say nothing about your weakness. Rorty, like his beloved Dewey, opposed the idea that everything in life must be justified before some ultimate tribunal — Truth, Reason, a higher law. Seen this way, one could say that part of our exhaustion comes from the feeling that our "musts" are set by the very nature of things. The language of endless productivity, for example, seems natural, though it is only one of the vocabularies of the age, not a law of the world. Pragmatism suggests asking of any "must": who needs it, and why? This doesn't cancel the real workload, but it can lift an extra burden — the feeling that rest has to be earned. Rest needs no metaphysical justification.
fatigue.practice: Pick one "I must" that is wearing you out and ask: to whom, exactly? What happens if, just for today, this "must" becomes "it would be nice to"?

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonising: everything is familiar, everything has already been said. Rorty called the kind of philosophy he liked "edifying" — its task is not to build a final system but to keep the conversation going, not letting it freeze. He loved the image of "the conversation of mankind", in which new voices and unexpected metaphors matter. Seen this way, one could say that boredom is the feeling that the conversation has run dry: all descriptions of the world have become habitual and no longer surprise. This isn't your fault; it is more like a hunger for new language. Rorty believed that novels, poems, other cultures and people unlike us can renew our vocabulary. Boredom, then, is not emptiness but an invitation: somewhere nearby there are words you haven't heard yet.
boredom.practice: Read one page of something quite outside your usual range — poetry, a scientific article, a stranger's blog. Note one word or thought that caught you.

joy.text: Joy needs no justification. In his essay "Trotsky and the Wild Orchids", Rorty recalled how as a teenager he passionately loved wild orchids and at the same time wanted to serve justice. He struggled for a long time to unite these two loves in a single theory, and in the end concluded that there was no need. Personal joy — in orchids, music, books — doesn't have to prove its social usefulness. Rorty distinguished the "private" (self-creation, one's own particular passions) from the "public" (reducing other people's suffering) and believed both have a right to exist. Seen this way, your joy can simply be accepted and lived — even if it seems strange, small or incomprehensible to others.
joy.practice: Name your "wild orchid" — something that delights you without being useful for anything. Give it at least a couple of minutes today.

love.text: Love and tenderness are neither weakness nor irrationality. Rorty believed that moral progress is driven less by arguments than by feelings: he spoke of "sentimental education", in which stories and closeness widen the circle of those we care about. In this sense, tenderness is the very material of moral life. Rorty described justice as enlarged loyalty: everything begins with love for particular people close to us, and can then grow. Seen this way, your love is not a private trifle against a background of "serious" matters but what all serious matters are made of. And its details — how a person laughs, what they love, what they fear — are exactly what makes them real to you.
love.practice: Tell or write to someone close to you one specific detail you love about them.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and Rorty gives it an interesting dimension. He stressed contingency: our language, our self and our community could have been quite different. Nothing we have was guaranteed by the laws of being. Rorty dreamed of a culture that no longer worships anything as a divinity, but this doesn't make gratitude unnecessary. One could say that gratitude is then directed to people and to chance: to those who gave us words, habits, support, and to a lucky turn of circumstances. Awareness of contingency doesn't devalue the good; it makes it sharper: it might not have happened, and yet it did.
gratitude.practice: Recall one word, thought or habit you received from a particular person. If you can, thank them — even if only in your mind.

hope.text: Hope is a key word for Rorty; one of his collections is called Philosophy and Social Hope. He believed that pragmatism replaces the search for final knowledge with hope: instead of asking "what is reality really like?" it asks "what future do we want, and can we build?" Such hope needs no guarantees. It doesn't rest on certainty that history is bound to move towards the better, but it doesn't give up in the absence of such certainty either. Rorty called this something like a "romance of the future". Seen this way, your hope is not naivety but a way of keeping the future open. It can be sustained with concrete images and small steps, without demanding promises from it.
hope.practice: Describe in two or three sentences one small future you would like — as concretely as possible, with details.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender and bitter longing for the past, and there is nothing wrong with it. Rorty wrote that people create themselves by redescribing their history. He referred to Nietzsche's thought of turning every "it was" into "thus I willed it": not denying the past, but finding one's own language for it. Seen this way, one could say that nostalgia is a longing not only for a time but also for a vocabulary in which the world once came together into an understandable picture. That vocabulary can't be brought back whole, but it can be reread. The past is not frozen: its meaning changes with each new telling. And what was dear can become a support for the present, not only a cause for sorrow.
nostalgia.practice: Recall a precious moment from the past and complete: "It gave me… and today it lives in me as…"

craving.text: A sharp craving — "I want it right now" — can be very strong, and there is nothing shameful in it. Rorty didn't write about cravings directly, but the pragmatism he drew on helps us look at them. Following William James, the pragmatists saw beliefs as habits of action. A craving speaks in a very confident language: "this is unbearable without it", "only this will help". From Rorty's point of view, one could say this is one description of the moment, not the final truth about it. The ironist knows how to notice: "right now this vocabulary is speaking in me." A craving is like a wave: it rises, peaks and subsides. If you name it differently and notice its beginning, a little room appears between the desire and the action.
craving.practice: Tell yourself: "A wave of desire is rising right now; it has a beginning and it will have an end." Note the time and watch how it changes over the next few minutes.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure and not proof of a "bad nature". Rorty didn't believe in a hidden "true self" at all, one that could turn out to be rotten deep down. For him, the self is a web of beliefs, desires and habits that has taken shape out of contingent circumstances. Such a web can't be rewoven in a day, but it can be retied gradually, thread by thread. From Rorty's point of view, one could add something else: we change not alone but within a "we". Communities of people who know this experience from the inside and talk about it in a shared language create the kind of solidarity he wrote about. A life organised around one thing can little by little grow new connections and new descriptions of oneself.
addiction.practice: Think about whether there is a person or a group where such experiences are talked about without judgement. You don't need to decide anything — just note that such places exist.

hangover.text: The morning after is hard: the body aches, and inside there is anxiety, shame, fragments of memories. Rorty wrote about how painful it is when a person is described in humiliating terms, and he considered cruelty the worst thing we do. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that the morning inner voice often speaks exactly this language: "I'm worthless", "everything is ruined". This is cruelty turned on oneself. The ironist knows that the harshest descriptions are not the final truth: this is one possible vocabulary, and right now it is louder than the others because you feel bad. You don't need to justify yesterday, nor to punish yourself. You can simply get through this morning, take care of yourself, and later, more calmly, decide what you want to understand from it.
hangover.practice: Write down the harshest sentence you are saying to yourself today. Then rewrite it the way you would say it to a friend on the same kind of morning.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, when everything seems possible. There's no need to spoil it with suspicion. Rorty admired the moments when a new language is born: new metaphors, in his view, are what suddenly let us see the world differently. He wrote about the "strong poet" who creates himself by finding words that didn't exist before. Euphoria can resemble such a moment: the world has suddenly been redescribed, and there is a lot of air in the new description. Seen this way, it's worth not only living it but also remembering a little of it: what words, images, thoughts came to you just now. The high will pass, as everything passes, but the words found in it may stay and prove useful later.
euphoria.practice: Write down one phrase or image this euphoria suggests to you. Keep it — not as a promise, but as a find.

crash.text: The drop after a high can be sharp and galling: a moment ago everything was shining, and now it's grey. Drawing on the philosopher Donald Davidson, Rorty described the life of metaphors: a new metaphor first astonishes, then becomes familiar and "dies", turning into an ordinary word. One could say there is a similar cycle in our experiences: what is vivid inevitably becomes ordinary. This doesn't mean the high was a deception and the drop the "real" truth. Neither of these states is the final description of your life. Rorty distrusted the words "actually, everything is…" with which we sum things up. The drop is one chapter, not the ending. You can give yourself time and avoid drawing big conclusions at the greyest moment.
crash.practice: Name one thing from the recent high that you'd like to keep. And one small act of care for yourself today.

panic.text: Panic is very frightening: your heart pounds, your breathing falters, and it seems something irreparable is about to happen. In such moments there's no room for theories, and that's normal. Rorty wrote that pain is something prior to language: it is what unites us with all people and even with animals. So the fact that words don't help right now is not your failure. A wave of panic usually builds, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. From the pragmatic point of view that Rorty held, it's useful to do what works right now and make sense of it later. Simply naming things brings us back into the shared world: the words we use together with others become a support again.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and breathe out for longer than you breathe in. Name, aloud or to yourself, five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what's the point of it all?" — can engulf you completely. Rorty honestly admitted that there is no answer to this question written into the structure of the universe, no "non-human authority" that guarantees meaning. But he didn't consider this a catastrophe. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that meaning was never hidden in the depths of the world: people have always created it together — in friendship, care, work, conversations, in attempts to make others' pain smaller. The absence of a guarantee from above doesn't cancel what is done here, between people. None of this requires a final answer tonight. You can let the question be — and lean on something small and close that matters to you simply because you care.
dread.practice: Write down one thing or one person that matters to you not because the universe says so, but simply because they are dear to you.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives is especially sharp in the age of feeds and photos. Rorty believed there is no one "right" or "best" life: there are many vocabularies in which people describe themselves, and none of them is final. Private self-creation, for Rorty, is idiosyncratic: everyone has their own path and their own "orchids". Seen this way, one could say that the fear of missing out often imposes someone else's vocabulary — "full", "successful", "at the centre of things" — as the only possible one. But we see other people's lives in their best description, and our own from the inside, with all its everyday details. You can notice this imbalance and ask yourself what "an interesting life" would mean in your own words.
fomo.practice: Complete the sentence: "For me, an interesting life is…" Try not to use a single word from the feed.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are a hard combination: darkness makes every thought enormous. Rorty taught us to notice the words we use to describe our lives. From his point of view, one could say that at night thoughts are especially fond of "final" language: "always", "never", "it's all lost". The ironist knows that no description — even one that is very convincing in the dark — is the last truth. The night vocabulary is only one of many, and in the morning it usually sounds different. You don't need to argue with every thought or settle everything before dawn. It's enough to note: "this is a night-time description" — and let it wait until morning, when there will be other voices and other words around.
sleepless.practice: If a thought won't let go, write it down and add at the end: "— this is a night-time description; I'll look at it again in the morning."

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but also the sense of "we". Rorty thought a lot about loyalty; he described justice as "enlarged loyalty" and said that our moral conflicts are often clashes between different loyalties. Seen this way, one could say that betrayal is the rupture of the "we" you were living in. Understanding the other person's motives doesn't have to justify anything: the pain and humiliation of betrayal are real, and Rorty considered them exactly what matters most not to inflict. But it also matters that a broken "we" doesn't cancel your capacity for trust. The fact that you knew how to be loyal remains yours, even if it wasn't valued.
betrayal.practice: Write down: what did this "we" give you, and what of it — the ability to trust, to care, to be there — do you want to keep in yourself?

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonising: the fear that you will be replaced, that there will be no room left for you in someone else's "we". Rorty stressed the contingency of our bonds: no attachment is guaranteed by the nature of things; everything could have turned out differently. That really can be frightening. But from Rorty's point of view one could also say something else: precisely because a bond isn't secured in advance, it is created and sustained — by attention, conversation, care. Jealousy shows how precious this bond is to you. There's no need to be ashamed of it. But you can examine it: what descriptions is it drawing — "I'm not as good", "I'll be left"? These are some of the possible stories, not proven facts. Sometimes it helps to test them through conversation rather than imagination.
jealousy.practice: Write down one story your jealousy is telling you. Mark what in it is known for certain and what has been filled in by fear.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a heavy burden, and it didn't come out of nowhere: you really were hurt. Rorty believed that we create ourselves by redescribing our history. From his point of view, one could say that resentment often clings to a single description of the past, repeated again and again in the same words. To redescribe is not to deny the harm or necessarily to forgive. It is to find other words for that story, in which you are not only the one who was hurt but also the one who goes on living. Rorty stressed that the past is not frozen: its meaning changes depending on how we tell it. The grievance can remain part of the story but stop being the whole story.
resentment.practice: Describe the old grievance in three sentences, the third beginning with the words: "And then I…"

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it deserves time. Reading Freud, Rorty described a person as a web of the finest, contingent connections: words, places, songs and habits weave together into what we call ourselves. Seen this way, one could say that the person you loved was woven into many threads of your web — and that is why the breakup echoes everywhere: in your routes, jokes, plans. This isn't weakness but evidence of how deeply you loved. The web doesn't tear forever; it gets retied, slowly, thread by thread. Something of what you received in this relationship will stay in you — as new words and ways of seeing the world.
heartbreak.practice: Name one thread that hurts most right now (a place, a song, a habit). Simply note it, without trying to get rid of it.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're about to be "found out" is familiar to a great many capable people. Rorty criticised the idea of knowledge as a mirror that accurately reflects reality. For him, knowledge and competence are what a community recognises as convincing in the course of practice and conversation, not a hidden essence that you might "actually" lack. Seen this way, one could say that impostor syndrome rests on an imaginary ideal image of the "real expert", compared with whom you are supposedly a fake. But there is no such image: there are people who learn, make mistakes and get the work done together. You are not a copy of a standard but a participant in this conversation, and your participation is already part of what makes the work work.
impostor.practice: Write down three concrete things you have already done well — not judgements, but facts. Who, besides you, could confirm them?

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is a very heavy feeling, and you don't have to agree with it. The inner critic speaks as if passing a final verdict. Rorty believed there are no final descriptions of a person: every description is only one of many, not the truth about your essence. He also said that cruelty is the worst thing we do, and that humiliation wounds especially painfully — when everything dear to you is made to look worthless. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that the inner critic does exactly this: it is cruel to you. And such cruelty can be treated the same way as cruelty to others: by refusing to grant that it is right. You deserve the same gentle treatment that you may well be ready to give to someone else.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic and ask yourself: would I let someone say this to my friend? If not, note that this sentence is cruelty, not truth.

helplessness.text: Being powerless to change something is one of the hardest experiences. Rorty was a realist: he didn't believe the world could be remade in one leap or by one great theory. He trusted gradual, partial improvements — the slow work of many people, each of whom does a little. Seen this way, one could say that helplessness is partly born of the feeling that everything should depend on you alone. But change, for Rorty, is always collective: it is made by many "we"s. This doesn't cancel the fact that right now there is much you cannot change. But it lifts from you the impossible task of changing everything. The hope he wrote about begins with something small — with one thing within your reach today.
helplessness.practice: Name one thing, however small, that is within your reach in the next hour. You don't have to do it — just notice that it is there.

procrastination.text: When you can't get started, it's easy to blame yourself for laziness, but it's usually not that simple. The pragmatists Rorty drew on — especially Dewey — saw thinking as an experiment: we try, see what happens, and correct. Seen this way, one could say that procrastination is often tied to waiting for the "right" beginning: the perfect plan, complete certainty, the final wording. But Rorty believed there are no final wordings at all — only working versions that improve along the way. Your first step doesn't have to be correct; it just has to exist, so that there is something to improve. A rough draft is not a failure but the normal form of any beginning.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and make the clumsiest possible draft of the first step. Allow it to be bad.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a deep experience: what collapses is not only daily life but also the language in which you were used to understanding the world. Rorty called "irony" the position of someone who has seen that their native final vocabulary is only one of many. Emigration often forces this experience on us: words that seemed natural at home don't work here. It hurts, and Rorty didn't say it was easy. But he stressed that "we" is not given forever: it can be widened and created anew. Seen this way, one could say that you live between vocabularies — and this is not only a loss but also a wealth: you know things that can be seen only from two shores. Roots can become not a single point but a web of connections.
uprooted.practice: Write down one word from your native language or place that is hard to translate. What does it mean to you?

overload.text: Overload and the endless feed are draining: it seems you have to manage to know about everything and have an opinion on it all. Rorty valued a multitude of voices and vocabularies, but he didn't think everyone was obliged to take them all in. He distinguished private life — your own passions and ways of creating yourself — from public life, where we try to reduce others' suffering. Seen this way, one could say that not every bit of informational noise requires your participation. The conversation of mankind that Rorty loved so much will go on without your hearing every word. You can choose: which voices truly enrich your vocabulary, and which simply take up space. Such selectiveness is not escape but care for your attention.
overload.practice: Name one source that truly enriches you and one that only wears you out. Set the second aside, at least for today.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be very frightening, and it deserves respectful attention. Rorty devoted Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature to criticising a picture in which the mind is an inner mirror, separated from the world by a veil of representations. It is in this picture that the question arises: is what I see real? Rorty, following Davidson, believed that we never lost touch with the world in the first place: we are in it — through the body, actions, conversations with others. Seen this way, one could say that even when the sense of reality is muted, you go on being in the world and among people. Simple actions and shared words help you return to this.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object and describe it aloud: weight, temperature, texture. Do one simple action — pour some water, open a window.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling. Rorty dreamed of a culture that worships nothing as a divinity, but he was no stranger to wonder. In an essay about his youth, he recalled spending long hours searching the mountains for wild orchids and being struck by their beauty. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that awe doesn't need a metaphysical explanation to be real. You can simply stand before a mountain, the sea, music or a human act and feel that it is bigger than you. Such a moment is worth not analysing but living, and perhaps finding words for — since new words, for Rorty, are exactly how we enrich life.
awe.practice: Describe what filled you with awe in one sentence — as if writing a postcard to a friend. Don't look for the right words; look for your own.

relief.text: Relief is like breathing out after long tension. You can simply live it. Rorty, following Wittgenstein and Dewey, loved the thought that some problems are not solved but dissolved: one day we notice that the question no longer holds us, because the description of the situation itself has changed. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that relief sometimes comes in just this way: not through a final answer, but because the heaviness has stopped being the main thing. This, too, is a real outcome. There's no need to start searching right away for what to do next. You can let yourself notice how your breathing, your shoulders, your gaze have changed — and thank yourself and others for getting through this.
relief.practice: Take a slow breath out and note where in your body the relief is felt. Keep your attention there for a few breaths.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and it doesn't need to be justified by anything. Rorty once spoke approvingly of philosophical "superficiality and light-mindedness": the ability not to demand final answers to big questions in order to live and act calmly. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that such calm is not indifference but freedom from the need to ground everything completely. The ironist knows that her vocabulary is not the last one, and so she can live without the constant strain of proving. The world doesn't have to come together into a single system right now. You can simply stay in this quiet moment — it is real, even if it settles nothing forever.
calm.practice: Spend a minute in silence and note three things that are not demanding any answer from you right now.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the moment when new words and images arrive. Rorty valued such moments above all: he believed that cultures and individuals grow through new metaphors, which at first seem strange and then change the way we see the world. He wrote about the "strong poet" — someone who creates himself by finding a language of his own instead of an inherited one. Seen this way, your inspiration is not a random flash but a share in the most important thing language can do: renew itself. You don't have to bring your ideas to perfection straight away. New metaphors are always clumsy at first and seem strange even to their author. What matters is to catch them while they're alive; they can be polished later.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down right now, as it is, even clumsily. Don't edit — just keep the living version.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is an awkward but very human feeling, and on its own it doesn't make you cruel. Following the philosopher Judith Shklar, Rorty considered cruelty the worst thing we do. But he distinguished the private from the public: a fleeting feeling inside is one thing, and an action that causes someone else pain is quite another. From Rorty's point of view, one could say that schadenfreude often appears when we see a person as "one of them" rather than "one of us". And solidarity, for Rorty, grows out of attention to the particular details of other people's pain. Schadenfreude can be used as an occasion: to imagine the concrete life behind someone's failure. Usually, after that, the feeling loses its force by itself.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine one concrete evening of the person who failed: where they are, what they feel. Notice what happens to your schadenfreude.

contempt.text: Contempt often protects us: it puts us above others so that it hurts less. Rorty saw clearly how people divide the world into "us" and "them" and how easy it is to deny "them" full humanity. We usually describe those we despise with one or two words: "idiot", "loser", "people like them". Rorty called such words a "final vocabulary" — the point beyond which our explanations don't go. The ironist, though, remembers that any vocabulary is only one possible description, and it can be revised. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: contempt is a description that has stopped. You don't need to force the feeling to change, but you can ask: what don't I know about this person's life? And what is my contempt protecting in me?
contempt.practice: Describe the person you feel contempt for in one sentence without evaluative words — only facts. What has changed?

disgust.text: Disgust is a powerful feeling, and it often protects: the body says "no" to what is unacceptable to you. Rorty stressed that many of our boundaries between "normal" and "disgusting" are not eternal truths but a legacy of history, culture and habit. In an essay on human rights he showed how easily people stop regarding others as fully human if those others repel them, and how stories and literature widen the circle of sympathy. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: disgust at a situation can be an honest signal, but disgust at people or at yourself is worth checking — whose vocabulary is it speaking? Not everything that repels is evil, and not every recoil tells the truth about you.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: is this disgust about something that really causes harm, or about something that is simply unfamiliar? Write down the answer.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural response to injustice. It says: I was treated cruelly, and that matters. Rorty considered cruelty the worst thing people do to one another, so your hurt is legitimate: you have run into exactly what he built his philosophy against. But something else follows from this too: revenge answers cruelty with cruelty and usually increases the amount of pain in the world. From Rorty's point of view, one could say there is a path stronger than revenge — to "redescribe" what happened so that the person who hurt you stops being the centre of your story. Your story belongs to you. You can decide what place this wound will take in it, and not give it the leading role.
revenge.practice: Write one sentence about what happened in which the protagonist is you, not the one who hurt you: "I went through…, and now I…"

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you is an ordinary part of any closeness, though people are often ashamed of it. Rorty greatly valued Freud for the idea that each of us contains several "selves", each with its own story, and that all of them are a legitimate part of a person. He wrote that Freud helped us see every human life as a poem woven from contingent events and memories. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: anger at someone close is not an exposure showing that you "actually" don't love them. It is the voice of one part of you, which has its own history and its own reasons. You don't have to choose between "I love" and "I'm angry". You can ask what the anger is saying, and put it into words without causing pain.
anger_at_loved.practice: Ask your anger, the way you would ask a friend: "What do you need?" Write down the answer in one sentence.

ambivalence.text: Loving and being unable to stand the same person at once is agonising, especially when it seems that one of the feelings must be "false". Rorty told a story about himself in the essay "Trotsky and the Wild Orchids": as a teenager he passionately loved rare orchids and at the same time wanted to fight injustice — and he struggled for a long time to fit these two loves into a single picture. Later he decided he didn't have to: a life may have no single common denominator. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: contradictory feelings for someone close don't need to be reduced to one "true" formula. Both sides can be the truth of your life. The ironist doesn't demand of herself a wholeness that isn't there. This doesn't make the relationship fake — it makes it human.
ambivalence.practice: Draw two columns: "what I love" and "what I find hard". Don't try to reconcile them — just let them stand side by side.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after an ending — a breakup, the end of a loved one's long illness — often arrives together with shame. This feeling is understandable, and it doesn't cancel love. Rorty believed that the "final vocabulary" we use to describe ourselves has largely come to us from other people and circumstances. Words like "a good daughter" or "a devoted husband" carry ideas about what one may and may not feel. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: relief seems shameful only as long as you describe yourself in other people's words. The same situation can be described differently: a long strain has ended, and you can finally breathe. Relief and love don't argue with each other — they are parts of one human story.
guilty_relief.practice: Describe your relief in one sentence, the way you would describe it for a dear friend who was in your place.

indifference.text: Sometimes you are not moved by what "should" move you, and it's frightening: am I a callous person? Rorty wrote about this in his chapter on Nabokov. He noticed that Nabokov's characters are sometimes cruel not out of malice but out of "incuriosity": they simply don't notice other people's pain. But Rorty has a gentle side too. He believed that sympathy is not an innate organ that you either have or don't, but something that grows through stories, details, attention. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: indifference is not a verdict on your soul. Perhaps you are tired, or something concrete was missing. The feeling may come when one living detail appears. Or it may not — and that is human too.
indifference.practice: Choose one detail of what isn't moving you — a name, a face, a circumstance. Stay with it for a minute, without demanding that you feel anything.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — is not a whim but a signal: the old description of your life no longer fits. Rorty believed that self-creation is the ability to tell a new story about yourself, to find new words for who you want to be. Following Harold Bloom, he wrote about the "strong poet" — someone who doesn't want to live their life by someone else's script. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: the wish to run away often means you have outgrown your old "vocabulary". But a life can be redescribed in different ways: sometimes you need to leave, and sometimes it's enough to name and arrange what you already have in a new way. The main thing is to understand which description you want to leave and which one you want to find.
escape.practice: Describe your life in one sentence as it sounds now. Then — as you would like it to sound. Which word has changed?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or "the wrong one" is bewildering: the feeling is there, but there's no room for it in your life. Rorty distinguished the private and public sides of life. In the private sphere, he believed, a person seeks their own language, their own desires and ways of self-creation; in the public sphere, what matters most is not causing pain to others. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: the attraction itself belongs to your private story and is not yet an action. It's no reason to shame yourself. But it can be interesting: what does this desire say about what you are missing, about who you want to become? You can study it the way you would read a novel about yourself — attentively, and without rushing to conclusions.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what word describes what draws me — not the person, but a quality? Write it down.

social_anxiety.text: The fear of people and their judgement can be very strong: it seems everyone is watching and judging. Rorty showed that "we" is not a given but something that is created. Solidarity, in his view, arises not from a common essence but from the ability to see another person as "one of us". From Rorty's point of view, one could say: in social anxiety you seem to see everyone else as "one of them" — judging, alien. But they too are most likely afraid of something, embarrassed, worried about the impression they make. Rorty believed that attention to the particular details of another's life widens the circle of "us". The fear of judgement can grow quieter if you remember: around you are people just as vulnerable as you.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time you're among people, notice a sign of nerves in someone — a gesture, a pause, an embarrassed smile. You are not the only one who feels nervous.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is draining: you want to know what will happen, and there is no knowing. Rorty believed that for centuries philosophy searched for firm foundations — an eternal truth to lean on. And he concluded that there are no such foundations: our language and our beliefs are contingent, formed historically, and could have been different. It sounds unsettling, but Rorty saw freedom in it. He proposed replacing the search for certainty with hope — the hope that the future can become better if we work on it. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: uncertainty is not a malfunction but the ordinary condition of human life. Without knowing the future, you can still choose what to hope for and what to do today.
uncertainty.practice: Replace the question "what will happen?" with "what do I hope for, and what can I do today?" Write down the answer.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — can drag on agonisingly. Following John Dewey, Rorty believed that thought exists not for contemplation but for acting and coping with life. From this pragmatic point of view, waiting is hard because it seems you can't act: everything is being decided somewhere else. But you can ask: what useful thing can I do now, while there is no answer? Sometimes it's preparing for different outcomes, sometimes it's turning to something else entirely. Rorty loved the image of an ongoing "conversation of mankind" whose outcome is not known in advance. Waiting is also part of the conversation, not an empty pause in life.
waiting.practice: Write two short plans: "if the answer is yes…" and "if it's no…". Then put them aside and do something else.

regret.text: Regret over something done or not done can refuse to let go for a long time. At the end of his life, gravely ill, Rorty wrote a short essay, "The Fire of Life". In it he admitted that he wished he had given more time to poetry — and he said it calmly, without self-punishment, as an honest observation. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: the past can be "redescribed". Not undone, but told anew, seeing in it not only mistakes but also what you could and couldn't do back then. The ironist knows that his former self spoke a different vocabulary. Then regret becomes not a verdict but material for a new story about yourself — and a hint about what matters to you now.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and then complete the sentence: "This shows that what matters to me is…"

quote.text: I now wish that I had spent somewhat more of my life with verse.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

longing.text: Longing for a particular person hurts in a special way: it is exactly them you miss, with all their particularities. Rorty believed that what makes people real to us is details — not general qualities, but the way a person laughs, what they say in the mornings, their favourite little words. Moral life, for Rorty, grows not from abstractions but from love for particular people. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: your longing is the other side of this particularity. You don't long for "a good person in general" but for exactly this person. And that is a sign of how real they were, or still are, to you. Longing is not weakness but a form of memory and loyalty.
longing.practice: Write down three details about this person that perhaps only you know.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can be very heavy. It is a sign that your circle of sympathy is wide. Rorty considered exactly this the main moral achievement: the ability to feel another's pain as something that concerns you too. He called the way to it "sentimental education" — through stories and the details of other people's lives. But Rorty was also a pragmatist: he suggested not drowning in general horror but looking for the concrete — particular people, particular tasks. Hope, for him, is not confidence in a good outcome but a readiness to work towards it. From his point of view, one could say: you are not obliged to carry all the pain of the world. Your response is the beginning of solidarity, not a reason for despair.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete, manageable action for someone who is having a hard time right now — even a very small one.

quote.text: …hope that suffering will be diminished, that the humiliation of human beings by other human beings may cease.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

rejection.text: Rejection wounds: it seems a final verdict has been passed on you. Rorty insisted that the world has no language of its own and passes no verdicts on our worth: "The world does not speak. Only we do." Every judgement is a description made by a particular person in a particular situation, in their words. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: when you were rejected, that was one description, not the truth about you. The other person was looking through their own "final vocabulary", in which there was no place for you. That hurts. But it doesn't mean there is no place for you anywhere. Your worth is not determined by one other person's description, and other descriptions exist too.
rejection.practice: Write down the words you use to describe yourself after the rejection. Then — the words someone who values you would use.

quote.text: The world does not speak. Only we do.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very strong, especially if you have been left before. Rorty believed that solidarity and closeness are not a given, found once and for all, but something created again and again: through attention, care, shared stories. On the one hand, this sounds unsettling: there are no guarantees. On the other, it gives hope: a bond can be built and strengthened; it isn't predetermined by fate. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: the fear of being abandoned is understandable, but it talks about the future as if it were already decided. And the future, for Rorty, is open. You can invest in the connections you have right now.
abandonment.practice: Recall one connection in your life that withstood a difficulty. What helped it hold?

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a pain full of silence: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. Rorty considered love for a particular person one of the deepest human experiences, from which all of moral life grows. But he was also clear-eyed: we cannot make another person share our vocabulary, our story, our feeling. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: your love is real and valuable in itself, even if it received no answer. It has shown what you are capable of: seeing another in detail, caring, hoping. The lack of an answer is not a verdict on you. It means your stories didn't coincide. That hurts, but it doesn't cancel your capacity to love.
unrequited.practice: Write down one thing you have learned about yourself thanks to this love.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the deepest wounds. Rorty considered it a special form of cruelty: to humiliate a person is to make what mattered to them look worthless. He analysed in detail Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the torturer seeks not simply to cause pain but to destroy the way a person understands themselves. That is exactly why, for Rorty, it's so important to remember: no language of description — neither yours nor anyone else's — is the final truth about a person. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: whoever humiliated you imposed their description on you. But you have a right to your own. The words in which you speak of yourself and your values can be reclaimed, little by little.
humiliation.practice: Write in a word or two what mattered to you before this humiliation — and still matters.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be very persistent: the mirror, photographs, other people's glances. It's a common feeling, and there's nothing shameful in it. Rorty showed that much of what seems to us a natural norm is actually a "final vocabulary" that has taken shape historically. Words like "beautiful", "proper", "too much" acquire meaning within a particular culture and era. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: your body is being judged in words that are not eternal truths. Once, quite different bodies were considered "beautiful" than today. You can notice where these words come from and try to describe your body differently: not as an object of judgement, but as what allows you to live, to hug, to move, to feel.
body_shame.practice: Describe your body in three words about what it does, not how it looks.

illness.text: Illness changes a great deal: the body you relied on lets you down, and familiar life shifts. Fear, anger and tiredness are legitimate here. Rorty wrote that pain is something "pre-linguistic": something that links us with all living creatures, even those that don't speak. So suffering is a shared experience, not a personal failure. No one is to blame for their body being ill. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: illness doesn't have to have a deep meaning or be a lesson, and it doesn't need to be justified with a beautiful description. But you are still the author of your story: you choose the words in which to tell of a life that includes illness. And illness is not the whole of your life.
illness.practice: Tell someone close to you, or write down, one thing that was hard today and one that was good.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a good, healthy feeling. You created something, endured something, saw something through. Rorty believed that people create themselves by finding their own words and their own deeds rather than repeating others'; he called this self-creation. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: pride is the moment when you recognise yourself in what you have done. Not because it is better than other people's, but because it is yours. Rorty didn't believe in eternal foundations or higher authorities: you don't need someone above to confirm the value of your work. It's enough that it matters to you and, perhaps, to the people around you. Let yourself be glad about it.
pride.practice: Tell someone what you are proud of — or write it down the way you would tell a friend.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a subtle feeling in which sorrow lives side by side with tenderness. Rorty greatly valued Proust — the writer who gazed into the past, into people and places that were gone, and recast them into a novel. For Rorty, Proust was a model "ironist": he didn't seek an eternal truth about himself but redescribed his life again and again until it became a work of art. Melancholy in this light is neither an illness nor a weakness. From Rorty's point of view, one could say: it is the moment when you look tenderly at what was and has passed, and it becomes part of your story. Such a feeling doesn't need fixing — it has a beauty of its own.
melancholy.practice: Write down in a few words one memory that resonates right now — as the beginning of a small story.
